summary: Specifies enhancements that let IP datagrams be routed to mobile nodes. A node keeps its home address while away, registers a care-of address with its home agent, and the home agent tunnels datagrams to it. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3344.

eli5.summary: Like having mail forwarded when you move: the post office at home sends your letters to wherever you are.

subtitle: How an IPv4 node keeps its address while moving between networks, with a home agent forwarding its traffic through a tunnel.

tldr.problem: In IPv4 an address identifies a point of attachment, so a node that moves must either change its address, breaking its connections, or have host-specific routes spread through the Internet, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A mobile node keeps a permanent home address and registers a care-of address with its home agent, which intercepts datagrams for the home address and tunnels them to the care-of address. Registration messages are authenticated to prevent remote redirection attacks.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can change their point of attachment without changing their IP address. RFC 5944 is the revised specification and replaces RFC 3344.

today: RFC 5944 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3344, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IPv4 Needs Mobility Support
sections.content:
IPv4 assumes that a node's IP address identifies where it is attached, so a node must sit on the network its address names or datagrams cannot reach it. To move without losing communication, a node could change its address, or host-specific routes could be spread through much of the Internet routing fabric. The RFC calls both often unacceptable: the first breaks transport and higher-layer connections when the node moves, and the second has severe scaling problems.

The protocol requirements are that a mobile node can keep communicating after changing its link-layer point of attachment without changing its IP address, that it can talk to nodes that do not implement mobility, and that all messages updating another node about the mobile node's location are authenticated to protect against remote redirection attacks. No changes are needed in hosts or routers that are not one of the new entities.

Because mobile nodes often use wireless links, the RFC also aims to keep administrative messages few and small. It treats Mobile IP as a solution to "macro" mobility, between IP subnets. For "micro" mobility such as handoff among nearby transceivers on the same subnet, link-layer mechanisms may be faster and cheaper.
sections.eli5: Normally your house number tells the postman exactly where you are. If you move and keep the same number, letters get lost. This RFC is a way to keep your number and still get your letters.

sections.title: Mobile Nodes, Home Agents and Foreign Agents
sections.content:
Mobile IP adds three entities. The mobile node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment between networks and keeps using its constant IP address. The home agent is a router on the mobile node's home network that tunnels datagrams to the node when it is away and tracks its current location. The foreign agent is a router on the visited network that gives routing services to the registered node and detunnels datagrams the home agent sent.

The mobile node has a long-term home address. When away, it also has a care-of address, the end of the tunnel toward it. There are two kinds. A foreign agent care-of address is an address of a foreign agent, so many mobile nodes can share it; the RFC prefers this mode because it does not strain the limited IPv4 address space. A co-located care-of address is a local address the node obtained itself, for example through DHCP, and the node then decapsulates tunneled datagrams on its own. That mode works without any foreign agent but needs a pool of addresses in the foreign network.

The flow is: datagrams for the home address reach the home network by normal routing, the home agent intercepts them and tunnels them to the care-of address, and the tunnel endpoint delivers them to the mobile node. In the reverse direction, datagrams from the mobile node generally use standard IP routing and need not pass through the home agent. The mobile node uses its home address as the source address of the datagrams it sends, apart from certain mobility management messages.
sections.eli5: You have a home address, like a permanent mailbox. When you travel, the helper at home forwards your mail to a temporary address, such as a hotel desk, and the hotel hands each letter to you.

sections.title: Agent Discovery
sections.content:
Agent discovery lets a mobile node learn whether it is on its home network or a foreign one, detect that it has moved, and find the care-of address a foreign agent offers. Mobile IP extends ICMP Router Discovery. An Agent Advertisement is an ICMP Router Advertisement with a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension (extension type 16) attached, and an Agent Solicitation is an ICMP Router Solicitation whose IP TTL MUST be 1. Advertisements also have TTL 1 and, if multicast, go to 224.0.0.1 or 255.255.255.255. No authentication is required for these messages.

The extension carries a Sequence Number, a Registration Lifetime (0xffff means infinity) and flag bits. Among them, R means registration is required even with a co-located care-of address, B means a busy foreign agent, H and F mark home agent and foreign agent service, and M and G show support for minimal and GRE encapsulation. At least one of F and H MUST be set, and an advertisement with F set MUST list at least one care-of address. A Prefix-Lengths Extension (type 19) may follow, and a one-byte padding extension (type 0) may be used to make the ICMP length even.

Agents that cannot be discovered through a link-layer protocol MUST send advertisements. All mobility agents MUST process packets sent to the Mobile-Agents multicast group, 224.0.0.11. Sequence numbers start at 0 after boot and each advertisement adds one, except that 0xffff is followed by 256, so a mobile node can tell a reboot (a drop into the range 0 to 255) from a rollover.

A mobile node can detect movement in two ways. One uses the ICMP Lifetime: if it hears nothing more from an agent within that lifetime, it assumes contact is lost. The other compares network prefixes from the Prefix-Lengths Extension. When it receives an advertisement from its own home agent, it has returned home and SHOULD deregister. Mobile nodes limit solicitations with binary exponential backoff, and MUST NOT register more than once per second on average.
sections.eli5: Helpers shout "I can help here!" at regular intervals, or answer when you ask. By listening, you work out whether you are home or visiting, and who can help.

sections.title: Registration Messages and Extensions
sections.content:
Registration is how a mobile node tells its home agent where it is, renews a registration, or deregisters on returning home. It creates or changes a mobility binding at the home agent, linking the home address to the care-of address for a lifetime. Control messages are sent over UDP to well-known port 434. The two message types are 1 (Registration Request) and 3 (Registration Reply).

If the node uses a foreign agent care-of address, it MUST register through that foreign agent, which relays the request to the home agent and relays the reply back (four messages). If it uses a co-located care-of address, it registers directly with the home agent (two messages), except that it SHOULD go through a foreign agent on the link when the R bit is set. A node that has returned home registers directly with the home agent.

The Registration Request carries flags S (retain prior bindings), B (forward broadcasts), D (the node decapsulates itself, meaning a co-located care-of address), M and G (alternate encapsulations) and T (reverse tunneling), plus a Lifetime, the home address, the home agent and the care-of address. A Lifetime of zero requests deregistration, and 0xffff means infinity. The 64-bit Identification field matches requests to replies and guards against replay. The Reply holds a Code. The home agent may grant a shorter lifetime than requested, and neither agent may increase the requested Lifetime.

Every request, and every reply from the home agent, MUST carry an authorization-enabling extension, which is always the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension (type 32). Two optional extensions cover the other pairs: Mobile-Foreign (type 33) and Foreign-Home (type 34). Extensions use a type-length-value format. Unrecognized types from 0 through 127 cause the message to be silently discarded, while those from 128 through 255 are ignored and the rest of the message is still processed. The RFC also defines long and short extension formats that add a sub-type.
sections.eli5: When you reach a new place, you send a short signed note to your helper at home saying "I am here now, please send my mail here for this long." The helper writes back to say yes or no.

sections.title: Routing and Tunneling
sections.content:
Home agents and foreign agents MUST support IP-in-IP encapsulation. A mobile node using a co-located care-of address MUST be able to receive IP-in-IP tunneled datagrams. Minimal encapsulation and GRE encapsulation are optional alternatives.

The home agent examines the destination of arriving datagrams, and for a mobile node registered away from home it tunnels each datagram to the registered care-of address. With multiple simultaneous bindings it tunnels a copy to each care-of address. When a binding lifetime expires the home agent deletes it without sending any reply, but keeps the node's other unexpired bindings. A foreign agent receiving a tunneled datagram for a node not on its visitor list silently discards it and MUST NOT send ICMP Destination Unreachable. It must also route datagrams from registered nodes, at minimum by checking the header checksum, decrementing the TTL and forwarding to a default router.

Broadcasts are forwarded only to nodes that set the B bit. For multicast, a node can join through a local multicast router on the visited subnet or through a bidirectional tunnel to its home agent. A mobile node may also be a router for a whole moving network.

For ARP, while a node is away its home agent MUST answer ARP Requests for it using proxy ARP, and MUST send a gratuitous ARP when it first registers a binding for the node. When the node returns, it MUST send a gratuitous ARP before sending its deregistration, and the home agent sends one when it accepts. While away, a mobile node MUST NOT broadcast ARP Requests or Replies.
sections.eli5: The helper at home grabs any letter addressed to you, puts it inside a bigger envelope addressed to your temporary place, and sends it. At the other end the big envelope is opened and you get the original letter.

sections.title: Authentication and Replay Protection
sections.content:
Registration redirects a node's traffic to a new address, which would be a serious vulnerability if it were not authenticated. ARP is also unauthenticated, so the gratuitous ARP the protocol relies on brings all of ARP's risks. Home agents and mobile nodes MUST be able to authenticate, and the default algorithm is HMAC-MD5 with a 128-bit key. The authenticator covers the UDP payload, all prior extensions and the Type, Length and SPI of its own extension. SPI values 0 through 255 are reserved. The RFC notes that the "prefix+suffix" use of MD5 is considered vulnerable.

The Identification field provides replay protection, and the style in use is part of the Mobility Security Association. All mobile nodes and home agents MUST implement timestamps, formatted like Network Time Protocol timestamps. A new timestamp must be greater than any earlier one from that node, and the home agent must find it close enough to its own clock. A default tolerance of 7 seconds MAY be used, and it SHOULD be greater than 3 seconds. A rejection uses Code 133 and returns the home agent's time so the node can resynchronize.

Nonces are optional. The home agent places a fresh nonce in the high-order 32 bits of the Identification field in each reply, and the mobile node returns it in its next request. If a registration fails because of an invalid nonce, the reply supplies a new one, so the protocol resynchronizes itself.

The RFC says that key distribution is difficult, so messages with the foreign agent are not all required to be authenticated. For users worried about ingress filtering, the RFC suggests reverse tunneling.
sections.eli5: Anyone could pretend to be you and tell your helper to send your mail somewhere else. So every note is signed with a secret code and stamped with the time, and the helper ignores old or unsigned notes.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 3344
sections.content:
Appendix F lists the changes made after RFC 3344. The Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension now shows more bit definitions that other documents had added, with citations. The home agent no longer has to send error replies to requests that failed because the foreign agent failed authentication, which makes it sturdier against denial of service attacks.

A foreign agent MUST use the Network Access Identifier to tell apart mobile nodes that share the same home address. It MUST NOT apply a Foreign-Home Authentication extension to a deregistration request. A new foreign agent error code, 194 (Invalid Home Agent Address), replaces the earlier use of 136 when the foreign agent does not serve the node as a home agent. A home agent that cannot support a requested nonzero unicast home address MUST reject with Code 129.
